transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I... I guess I'm here because things at the lab are just completely falling apart, and it's my fault, really, because I can't seem to focus on the actual experiments anymore. It's like my brain is just pulling in every single direction all at once. For example, just last week, we were having this incredibly important grant call with the funding agency, and I was supposed to be presenting the preliminary data, but right in the middle of it, I noticed this faint, rhythmic vibration coming from one of the vacuum pumps down the hall. I mean, nobody else seemed to hear it, or if they did, they didn't care, but to me, it was like a siren, and I started thinking about the mechanical tolerances and whether the bearings were failing, and before I knew it, I had completely lost the thread of the grant call. 

And it's not just that! In our weekly safety meetings, which are supposed to be straightforward, a grad student will make some offhand comment about a solvent extraction, and suddenly I'm thinking about this odd, unexplained peak I saw in an NMR spectrum from, like, three years ago. I'll just get up and go chase down that old file, tearing through directories for hours, completely obsessed with figuring out what that peak was, while the entire team is sitting there waiting for me to approve the new protocol. The things everyone actually needs from me—the approvals, the data analysis, the grant writing—it's all just piling up and falling apart because I keep getting hijacked by every little sound, comment, or random thought that crosses my path. I just can't filter anything out anymore, and it's exhausting, honestly.
Do you find yourself repeating certain actions or rituals over and over?

Rituals? Um... no, no, not really. I mean, when you say rituals, I think of something structured, you know? Like... like someone who has to check the fume hood sash exactly three times before leaving the lab, or someone who organizes their pipette tips in a very specific, rigid way every single morning. I don't do anything like that. 

Actually, it's—it's almost the exact opposite for me right now. My lab manager is constantly frustrated with me because I absolutely lack any routine or repetition anymore. I used to be so methodical. I used to have this whole sequence for how I'd calibrate the mass spectrometer every Tuesday, down to the exact way I'd prep the blanks and log the baseline drift in the physical notebook before even touching the software. I had a system. But lately? I can't even get myself to do the same thing twice if I tried. I'm just bouncing from a beaker to a spreadsheet to a random email from 2019. There's no pattern to it, no repetition at all. It's just this chaotic forward momentum... or sideways momentum, really. 

So, no, I don't find myself repeating actions over and over. I kind of wish I did, honestly, because maybe then I'd actually have some sort of anchor or structure to my day, but no, it's just a constant, unpredictable scramble.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge?

Anxious? No, I wouldn't say anxious. I mean, when I think of being anxious or on edge, I think of people who are, you know, worried about bad things happening, or they have this pit in their stomach about the future, or they're scared of making a mistake. Like my sister, she's always anxious, always fretting about her kids' grades or whether she left the stove on, just constantly wound up tight with worry. But that's not me at all. 

If anything, I feel... I feel the opposite of worried. I feel like everything is incredibly urgent and important, but not in a scary way. It's more like there's this electric current running just under my skin, and it's pushing me, constantly pushing me to do more, see more, figure things out. Like, I don't feel on edge like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop. I feel on edge like I'm standing at the starting line of a race and I just need the gun to go off so I can run. 

I guess the only time I feel something close to what you might call "on edge" is when people are moving too slowly, which is all the time lately. Like yesterday, I was trying to explain to the post-doc why we needed to completely restructure the data pipeline for the new assay, and he was just staring at me, blinking, taking forever to process what I was saying. And I could feel my heart beating faster, and my muscles getting tense, but it wasn't anxiety. It was just pure, unadulterated frustration that the rest of the world is operating on dial-up while my brain is on fiber optics. So, no, I don't feel anxious or worried about things going wrong. I just feel incredibly, overwhelmingly energized, and maybe a little impatient when reality can't keep up with me.
Do you often find yourself talking more than others in social situations?

Talking more than others? Um... no, I really don't think so. I mean, when you look at the people I work with, especially the principal investigators or even just the administration folks, they absolutely love to hear themselves talk. If anything, I feel like I'm the one who has to sit there and wait for them to finish! 

Like, just last Friday, we had this sort of impromptu gathering in the breakroom for a colleague's birthday—Dr. Aris from the optics lab, he was turning fifty or something—and everyone was just standing around eating this terribly dry grocery store sheet cake. And they were just droning on and on and on about the new parking permit system on campus. Which, yes, is a complete logistical nightmare, I'll give them that, but they were taking twenty minutes to say what could literally be summarized in two sentences. I actually barely said a word during that whole thing! I was just standing there, shifting my weight, thinking about how incredibly inefficient the whole conversation was. 

When I do speak, I just get straight to the point. I mean, I have to, right? Because there is just so much information to convey and so little time to actually do it. So I might speak, you know, a bit more efficiently, or I might just be trying to push the conversation forward because everyone else is dragging their feet, but taking up more airtime than other people? No, definitely not. I don't dominate the conversation just for the sake of chatting. I'm usually just standing there waiting for everyone else to finally get to the point so we can all move on to something that actually matters.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or having trouble sitting still?

Fidgeting? No. No, I don't fidget. When you say fidgeting, I immediately picture, you know, the undergrads I used to TA for. You look out over the lecture hall and there's always that one kid in the third row who is just bouncing his knee so hard the entire table vibrates, or they’re clicking those multi-colored pens—click, click, click—just completely vacant, staring off into space. That’s fidgeting. It’s like this useless, nervous leakage of energy because they don't know what to do with themselves. 

I don't do that. I don't tap my foot, I don't twirl my hair, I don't pick at my fingernails. If I need to sit, I can sit. It’s just that... well, I don't really *choose* to sit all that much right now, because why would I? There is just an immense amount of actual, physical work to be done in the lab. So if I'm up and moving around, it’s not because I have "trouble" sitting still, like it’s some kind of physical limitation or a problem. It’s because sitting still would be completely counterproductive. 

Like on Wednesday, I was running the spectrophotometer, and instead of just sitting there in the rolling chair waiting for the readout like everyone else does, just mindlessly scrolling on their phones, I was up checking the inventory on the solvent cabinets, and then I was cross-referencing the safety data sheets for the new shipment of reagents we got, and then I was over at the whiteboard mapping out the next three weeks of assays. I was in constant motion, sure, but every single movement had a distinct purpose. It was highly efficient. 

So, no, I don't have trouble sitting still, and I certainly don't fidget. I just choose to be in motion because that's where the work gets done, you know? I don't see any reason to just sit around when I'm this dialed in.
Are you finding it difficult to fulfill your responsibilities at work or in your personal life due to these distractions and constant shifts in focus?

Well, "difficult" is a very loaded word. I personally don't find it difficult at all, because like I said, I am incredibly dialed in right now. I am seeing connections in our research that nobody else is seeing. But if you were to ask the administration, or the department chair... well, they have a completely different, and frankly, very frustrating perspective on the whole situation. 

It’s actually been a massive headache this past week because my department has recently had to step in on decisions that I used to handle completely on my own. And I’ve been managing these protocols for years! But suddenly, because my brain is moving at a pace they can't comprehend, they’re claiming I have all these "missed priorities." Which is just absurd. I didn't miss any priorities; I simply realized that the original timeline we set in January was completely obsolete based on the real-time data I was pulling, so I pivoted the entire focus of the lab. I bypassed some of the standard, redundant reporting because it was slowing me down, and they panicked.

And then they brought up what they called "confused scheduling." I spent twelve hours completely revamping the equipment booking system to maximize our throughput—literally color-coding a new calendar system so the mass spec wouldn't sit idle for even a minute—but apparently, nobody else could understand it. The post-docs were complaining they didn't know when their bench time was, which led to the department accusing me of "strained supervision." Like, I’m sorry that I expect my team to actually keep pace with me and adapt to a more efficient system instead of needing their hands held every step of the way! 

So now, because they can't handle the pace I'm setting, they’ve stepped in and started requiring committee approval for things I used to just sign off on. They actually sat me down and had the nerve to tell me that my actions were putting the entire project at risk. They even brought up lab safety expectations! Just because I left a few volatile reagents out on the active bench overnight so they'd be primed and ready to go the second I walked back into the lab the next morning. It wasn't a danger to anyone, it was a calculated efficiency! But they completely overreacted. So, no, *I* am not finding it difficult to do my job, but I am finding it incredibly difficult to do my job while my own department is constantly breathing down my neck and stripping away my autonomy just because they're too slow to keep up.
Are you feeling overwhelmed or distressed by your inability to focus and constant distractions?

Distressed? Overwhelmed? No, absolutely not. I mean, I think the premise of your question is flawed, to be honest. You're assuming that I have an "inability to focus" and that I'm suffering from "constant distractions." But that's just not what's happening here. I'm not distracted; my focus is just incredibly broad and... and dynamic right now. 

If anything, the only thing that distresses me—and "distress" is probably the wrong word, it's more like a profound irritation—is how painfully slow everything else is. Like, my brain is operating on this entirely different frequency. I'm processing data, connecting variables, visualizing the entire architecture of our current study all at once. It's exhilarating! I feel like I've finally tapped into the actual capacity of my intellect. Why would I be overwhelmed by that? It’s like finally driving a sports car on an open highway after being stuck in rush hour traffic in a beat-up sedan for ten years. 

The only overwhelming part is dealing with everyone else's limitations. Like yesterday, I was trying to explain to my lead tech—who is usually quite competent, by the way, he’s been with me for three years—I was trying to explain how we could completely restructure the control group parameters based on this flash of insight I had while I was re-calibrating the centrifuge. And I’m laying it all out, drawing on the glass wall of the office because the whiteboard was already full of my notes from the morning, and he just stared at me. Just blankly stared. And then he had the audacity to ask me to "slow down and go back to step one." Step one! We were already on step ten in my head. 

So, no, my mind moving fast isn't distressing at all. It's brilliant. It's productive. The only distress comes from the friction of having to constantly hit the brakes so the rest of the world can catch up. I just wish everyone else could operate at this level, you know? The things we could accomplish if they didn't need everything spoon-fed to them at a snail's pace.
Are you having trouble getting along with friends or family because of your current state of mind?

Friends and family? I mean, honestly, I barely even talk to my family right now because there simply aren't enough hours in the day, and my focus is entirely on the work. My sister did call me on Sunday and told me I was being "hostile" just because I asked her to please get to the point of her story since I was in the middle of analyzing a dataset, but... well, that's just her being overly sensitive. 

The real friction, if you want to talk about getting along with people, is happening at the lab. And it's so frustrating because for months—literally for months now—I've felt like the lab is finally, finally moving at my speed. It is almost electrified in there for me. I walk in and I can just feel the current of productivity, the sheer potential of what we're doing, and my brain is just firing on all cylinders. 

But nobody else seems to feel it! And that is where the problem is. Because if someone questions my plan, or if they have the nerve to ask me to slow down so they can catch up to what I'm doing, I... well, I snap at them. I just snap. Like yesterday, one of the undergrads asked why I was restructuring the assay sequence, and I just lost it. I don't have the time or the tolerance for people questioning a methodology that is clearly superior just because they're used to doing things the slow, outdated way. 

And I guess I've been snapping at them in a way that's pretty intense, because I've started to notice that the students are completely avoiding my office. Like, they will literally walk down the opposite hallway to get to the breakroom so they don't have to pass my open door. I saw one of them peek around the corner, see me at my desk, and actually turn around and walk the other way. Which, frankly, I consider a win because it cuts down on the meaningless chatter and the constant interruptions, but I suppose if you're asking if I'm having trouble getting along with people... yes. But it's only because they are constantly trying to put the brakes on when I am finally operating at full capacity. I just don't have the patience to coddle people who can't keep up with the current.
Have you been having trouble sleeping or noticed any changes in your sleep patterns lately?

Trouble sleeping? No, no, no. Again, you're using this negative framing, like there's a problem or a deficit. I don't have *trouble* sleeping, I just don't *need* to sleep the way other people do right now. It's actually been an incredible optimization of my time. 

If we're talking about the actual hours, then yes, there's been a change. Most nights I sleep two or three hours, tops. But it's not because I'm tossing and turning or struggling. It's just that I have so much to do, and the ideas are so clear, that stopping feels completely counterproductive. What usually happens is I'll leave the lab—usually because security does their final rounds and practically begs me to go home—and I'll immediately set up on my living room couch. I'll have my laptop open, running the statistical models that the lab computers were too slow to finish, and I'll just keep working. And eventually, maybe around 3:30 or 4:00 in the morning, my body will just sort of power down for a minute. I'll fall asleep right there on the couch, laptop still open on my lap, screen still glowing. 

But the amazing thing is, when I wake up two or three hours later, I am completely sharp. I don't have that groggy, hitting-the-snooze-button phase that normal people have. I just open my eyes, look at the code on my screen, and I am instantly ready to work. I don't feel tired at all! Not even a little bit. I just pick up the exact train of thought I had when I drifted off. 

Honestly, I've come to realize that the standard eight hours of sleep everyone insists on is just a completely inefficient interruption. Think about how much time people waste just lying there in the dark, unconscious, doing absolutely nothing! It's a third of your life! When you have the kind of momentum I have right now, when the variables are just aligning perfectly in your mind, forcing yourself to power down and go lie in a bed is just a massive waste of time. I actually resent the fact that human biology requires any sleep at all, frankly, but getting it down to a two-hour power nap on the couch has been a total game-changer for my productivity. I've accomplished more between midnight and 6 AM this past week than my entire department has in a month. So no, I'm not having "trouble." I'm just not wasting time being unconscious.
Have you experienced any significant problems at work or in your personal relationships as a direct result of your current behavior?

Problems? I mean, if you ask the department chair—who hasn't touched a pipette or run a gel in fifteen years, by the way—he’d probably use that exact word. But I call it a difference in visionary scope. It’s entirely a matter of perspective. 

But, to answer your question directly, yes, there has been... a situation. Let me give you the full context because it’s honestly ridiculous. So, my department, the administrative higher-ups, they’ve actually had to step in recently. They literally stepped in and took over decisions that I have handled flawlessly, without any oversight, for the last five years. 

And do you know what their justification was? They sat me down in this incredibly patronizing meeting and claimed I had "missed priorities." Missed priorities! Just because I decided to pivot the primary focus of our grant toward the secondary variable—because the data was absolutely screaming at me to do it, it was so obvious—but to them, that's a missed priority because it wasn't on their rigid little quarterly checklist. 

And then they started in on my calendar, saying I was creating "confused scheduling." Look, just because I booked the electron microscope at 3:00 AM and expected the team to be there... I mean, that is the only time the ambient vibrations in the building are low enough for the resolution I need right now! I had three different assays running concurrently, and yes, maybe I double-booked the prep room a few times, and maybe I forgot to cancel a faculty meeting because I was in the middle of a breakthrough, but a competent, dedicated team would have just adapted. 

Instead, because of that, and because of what I mentioned earlier about the students acting like I'm radioactive and avoiding my office, the department claimed my supervision has become "strained." Strained supervision! That was the exact phrase they used. 

So now, because they can't keep up, they’re claiming that my methods are putting the entire project at risk. They even brought up lab safety expectations. Safety! I bypassed one—literally one—redundant ventilation check last week because I was working with standard, low-volatility reagents and I didn't have forty-five minutes to wait for the automated clearance cycle to finish. It was perfectly fine. I calculated the parts-per-million dispersal in my head in two seconds, it was well below the threshold. But because I didn't log it in their archaic three-ring binder, suddenly I'm a safety risk putting the lab in jeopardy. 

So now they’ve temporarily reassigned my core project management duties. They’re making the day-to-day decisions I used to handle with my eyes closed. It is incredibly insulting. I am trying to revolutionize our entire methodology, I am giving them the best work of my career, and they are punishing me for it because they are terrified of a little procedural agility. So, yes, I suppose there are "problems" at work, but the problem is their bureaucratic red tape, not my behavior.
Have you lost any friendships or had any significant relationships end because of your current behavior?

Lost friendships? No. No, absolutely not. I mean, you have to actually be participating in a social life to lose it, right? Nobody has dramatically walked out of my life or cut ties with me, if that’s what you’re looking for. 

Honestly, my friends—most of whom are in the sciences anyway, or at least academia-adjacent—they know how I get when I’m on the verge of something big. They know that when I’m in the zone, I just drop off the radar. Like my friend Elena, she texted me last week about getting coffee, and I just replied with a picture of my spectrophotometer readings and said, "Talk in a month." And that was that! She didn't get mad, she didn't end the friendship. She just sent back a thumbs-up emoji. Because reasonable people understand that you don't interrupt a major intellectual breakthrough for a forty-five-minute chat over lattes. 

So no, I haven't lost anyone. I just... I don't have the bandwidth for the mundane maintenance of a social circle right now. I don't have the patience to sit around discussing television shows or whoever's kitchen remodel is happening, because my mind is operating on a completely different plane. It's just a matter of resource allocation. My energy is going into the data, not into small talk. 

If anything, my friends are just in a holding pattern. They're waiting for me to slow down and come back to their level, which, frankly, I have no intention of doing anytime soon because I have never felt this sharp. But as far as actual relationships ending? No, not at all. My sister is annoyed, like I mentioned before, but she's still my sister, she's not going anywhere. Everyone is still exactly where they were. I’m just too busy actually accomplishing things to entertain them right now.
Do you feel that your current way of thinking and behaving is causing you any significant problems or distress in your daily life?

Distress? I mean... I wouldn't use the word distress, because that implies I'm sitting around crying about it, which I'm definitely not. But... look, if I'm being completely honest with you, there is a reason I actually came in today. It's not because of the sleep, and it's certainly not because my department chair doesn't understand my methods. 

It's... well, it's because I can't keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. The primary one, I mean. The one that actually has the funding attached to it. 

I have all this incredible momentum, but my attention is just... it's like a laser beam that won't stay mounted on the target. I'll be right in the middle of something critical—like a major grant call with the funding agency, or sitting in one of those excruciating mandatory lab safety meetings—and something will just catch my attention. Like, I'll notice a subtle pump vibration coming from the centrifuge in the next room. Not a normal hum, but a slight, rhythmic acoustic anomaly that means the bearings are off by maybe a millimeter. Or one of the grad students will make some completely offhand side comment about a solvent gradient, or I'll just be scrolling through my files and I'll spot some odd peak in an old mass spectrum from three years ago. Just a tiny, insignificant blip that we wrote off as background noise back in 2020. 

And suddenly, that's it. That is the most important thing in the universe. I'm completely consumed by it. I'll just drop whatever I'm doing and I'm off chasing that odd peak or that pump frequency for hours and hours. I'll pull up a dozen different databases, write a completely new script to analyze the vibration frequencies, totally ignoring the fact that I'm supposed to be leading a grant call. And the worst part is, the tangential work I'm doing is brilliant! It's amazing! But while I'm doing it, the actual thing everyone needs from me—the primary data synthesis, the approvals, the actual project—it just completely falls apart. 

So, yes, I suppose that is a problem. It's incredibly frustrating because I know exactly what I *should* be doing, but the moment one of those little details pops up, I just physically cannot stop myself from going down the rabbit hole, and everything else just disintegrates.
Do you think your current behavior is significantly impacting your ability to function effectively in your job or personal life?

Well, I feel like I just went over this with you, didn't I? The whole situation with the administration? When you ask if it’s impacting my ability to function... look, *I* am functioning at a level most people can only dream of. My mind is firing on all cylinders, I am seeing connections in the data that no one else is seeing. 

But if you mean, is it impacting my job in a practical, administrative sense because of how *other* people are reacting to my methods? Then, yes, obviously. Like I was explaining just a few minutes ago, it has become this massive, incredibly frustrating ordeal because my department has actually stepped in on decisions that I used to handle completely on my own. For five years, I managed that lab flawlessly, and now suddenly they feel the need to micromanage me. 

And it all comes back to what I was telling you about their ridiculous justifications. They are using things like my "missed priorities"—which is just me pivoting to more important data—and the "confused scheduling"—which, again, is just me optimizing the equipment usage at 3:00 AM—as ammunition against me. They literally sat there and told me that because of all that, and because of the "strained supervision" with the students who can't keep up with my pace, I am somehow a liability. 

They actually claimed that I am putting the entire project and our lab safety expectations at risk! Putting it at risk! It’s just so incredibly insulting. I bypass one redundant ventilation check because I can do the math in my head faster than their archaic machines can clear the room, and suddenly I'm this huge danger to the university. 

So, yes, my ability to function in my job *as they define it* is being significantly impacted, but only because they've stripped away my autonomy. They've taken over my day-to-day decisions because they are terrified of my momentum. It’s like putting a speed governor on a Formula One engine just because you’re afraid of how fast it can go. I am trying to hand them a career-defining breakthrough on a silver platter, and they are punishing me for it by tying my hands with bureaucratic red tape. So, yes, there is an impact, but the problem isn't my ability to function. The problem is their inability to let me work.
Do you feel like you're acting on impulse when you switch between tasks or pursue new ideas?

Impulse? No, I wouldn't call it impulsive. "Impulse" makes it sound like I’m just... randomly grabbing at shiny objects without any underlying logic, like a child in a toy store. That’s not what this is at all. It’s not an impulse, it’s an absolute, overwhelming necessity to maximize my output while my mind is working at this level. 

You have to understand what my mornings look like right now to really get it. I am at the lab hours before anyone else even arrives. I’m talking 4:00 AM, the building is completely dark, the security guard is still doing his rounds, and it's just me and the hum of the HVAC system. And I am doing the work of ten people because I finally have the clarity to see how everything connects. I'm sitting at my workstation, and I'm rewriting our entire set of extraction protocols from scratch because the ones the department gave us are hopelessly inefficient. And while I'm compiling that, I've got another window open and I'm completely rearranging the instrument schedules—the mass spectrometers, the NMR machines—optimizing the run times so there is absolutely zero downtime for the equipment. 

And that's just the administrative side! At the exact same time, I'm drafting and firing off emails to our international collaborators. I'm messaging the team in Leipzig about their catalyst data, I'm coordinating with a lab in Kyoto, I'm talking to a research group in Oxford—three different countries, managing all those time zones in my head without missing a beat. And I'm starting entirely new statistical analyses on the raw data we pulled last month, running the scripts simultaneously while I type. 

So, it's not that I'm impulsively jumping from task to task because I lack discipline. It's that I am doing all of it at once. I *have* to do it all at once. Because if I just sit still and force myself to focus on one single, plodding task like everyone else expects me to... it physically feels like I am wasting this incredible window. It feels like I'm throwing away the one chance I have to finally fix everything that's broken in our methodology and our data pipeline. I have this immense capacity right now, and sitting idle or slowing down to a normal, linear pace just feels like a complete betrayal of the science. So, no, it's not an impulse. It's just a perfectly calibrated, high-speed execution of everything that needs to get done.
Do you feel like your current behavior is causing you significant distress or impairment in your ability to function socially or occupationally?

I feel like we are going in circles here. Are you... did you not hear what I said earlier? Because I literally just went over this exact thing with you not ten minutes ago. I just told you all about the administration and how they're reacting! 

But fine, if you need me to repeat myself for your notes, yes, there is an "impairment" occupationally, but it is entirely an impairment imposed on me by other people. Like I already explained, my department has had to step in on decisions I used to handle completely by myself. For years, I was the sole decision-maker for my team. I managed the budgets, the equipment rosters, the chemical inventory, the grant timelines, all of it, flawlessly. And now? Now I have the department chair literally CC'ing himself on my emails to the post-docs and requiring dual sign-offs for basic reagent purchases! 

And why? Because of their complete inability to keep up with my pace. They keep throwing around these bureaucratic buzzwords, claiming my "missed priorities"—which, again, is just me pivoting to far more groundbreaking data—and my "confused scheduling" are causing chaos. It is so absurd. Just because I double-booked a fume hood at 2:00 AM so I could run a parallel synthesis doesn't mean the schedule is confused, it means the schedule is finally being maximized! 

But they don't see it that way. They keep bringing up this "strained supervision" nonsense, whining that the graduate students are exhausted and overwhelmed by my directives. Well, maybe the students just need to work harder! Maybe they need to rise to the occasion! But instead of recognizing that I am pushing this team to greatness, the administration decided that all of this is somehow putting the primary project and our lab safety expectations at risk. 

They actually brought up safety! To me! I wrote half the safety protocols for that wing of the building when they were first built! They act like I'm going to blow up the centrifuge just because I'm bypassing a few redundant checklists that take up too much time. So yes, my occupational functioning is currently a massive, frustrating nightmare, but not because my brain isn't working. It's because they've decided my methods are a liability, panicked, and completely hijacked my lab.
Do you think your constant shifting of focus and attention to different tasks is causing you significant problems in your daily life?

Look, I know I just spent all this time defending my methods, and I stand by that—my output is absolutely incredible right now. But... if I am being completely honest with you, and this is actually the real reason I finally agreed to come in and see you today... it is getting to be a double-edged sword. Because the truth is, I just can't keep my mind on the actual, primary experiment anymore. 

It’s like my filter is completely gone. I will be sitting there, right in the middle of a critical, multi-million dollar grant call with the funding agency, or... or I'll be forced to sit through one of those agonizingly tedious safety meetings the department chair is suddenly making me attend. And I'm trying to focus, I really am, but then I'll hear it. Just this tiny, almost imperceptible pump vibration coming from the lab next door. Or one of the second-year students will make some completely offhand, throwaway side comment about a solvent gradient. Or, even worse, I'll just happen to glance over at my secondary monitor and notice this one odd, anomalous peak in an old mass spectrum from three years ago that we never fully resolved.

And the moment that happens, it's over. That one tiny detail just hooks into my brain and pulls, and suddenly I am off chasing that specific anomaly for hours. I'll literally walk right out of the safety meeting to strip down the vacuum pump, or I'll spend six hours writing a new script to cross-reference that old spectrum against our current database. And I'm making brilliant connections, I really am, but... meanwhile, the grant call is still happening without me. The primary experiment, the actual deliverable that the entire department and all our collaborators desperately need from me in that exact moment... it just completely falls apart. I leave them hanging, and the whole project stalls because I got entirely derailed by a pump vibration. So, yes. It is causing problems. Huge problems.
Do you feel that your inability to stay focused on one task is causing you significant distress or problems in your daily life?

I feel like I'm in the Twilight Zone right now. I literally *just* answered this exact question. Did you... did you not hear the entire story I just told you about the vacuum pump? Or the grant call? Are you just reading off a standardized checklist and not actually listening to the words coming out of my mouth? Because I just spent I don't know how many minutes explaining in excruciating detail how my inability to stay on the primary experiment is derailing everything!
